The photocurrent **rises and then saturates** as the anode is made more positive, and it
reaches zero at the **stopping potential**.
**Step 1 — start at the negative end.** At a sufficiently negative anode potential, even
the fastest photoelectron is turned back and the current is **zero** ✓ The least
negative potential at which this happens is the **stopping potential −V₀**, so the curve
must meet the axis there.
**Step 2 — move towards zero.** As the retarding voltage is reduced, slower electrons
begin to reach the anode and the current **rises** ✓ At zero applied voltage there is
already a current, since some electrons reach the anode under their own kinetic energy.
**Step 3 — go positive.** A positive anode attracts the electrons, collecting a larger
fraction of them, so the current continues to rise ✓
**Step 4 — reach saturation.** Once **every** emitted electron is collected, no further
increase is possible, and the curve **flattens** at the saturation current ✓
**Step 5 — match to the graphs.** The curve must start at zero at −V₀, rise smoothly,
and level off - which is **Graph I** ✓
**Why the current saturates.** It is limited by the **number of photoelectrons emitted
per second**, which depends only on the light's intensity ✓ No voltage can collect more
electrons than the surface releases.
**What sets each feature.**
the **stopping potential −V₀** depends on the light's **frequency** and the work
function, through eV₀ = hν − φ ✓
the **saturation current** depends on the light's **intensity** ✓
The two are completely independent - which is the central surprise of the photoelectric
effect.
**Why the other graphs fail.**
**Graph II** ✗ rises **without limit**, ignoring saturation.
**Graph III** ✗ shows the current **falling** as the anode becomes more positive, the
reverse of the physics.
**Graph IV** ✗ rises ever more steeply, again with no saturation ✓
**What a second curve would show.** Brighter light of the same colour would saturate at
a **higher** current but meet the axis at the **same** −V₀ ✓ Light of higher frequency
at the same intensity would do the opposite - same saturation, more negative V₀.
∴ Graph-I.

All electromagnetic waves travel at the **same speed** in vacuum; what distinguishes
them is their **wavelength** and frequency.
**Step 1 — recall the speed.** In free space every electromagnetic wave travels at
c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) = **3 x 10⁸ m s⁻¹** ✓
The expression contains no reference to frequency, so the speed is the same for X-rays,
gamma rays and microwaves alike.
**Step 2 — see what differs.** They are distinguished by frequency and wavelength,
linked by
c = νλ ✓
with the product fixed, so a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.
**Step 3 — place the three.**
**gamma rays**: λ below 10⁻¹² m, ν above 10²⁰ Hz
**X-rays**: λ about 10⁻¹² to 10⁻⁸ m
**microwaves**: λ about 10⁻³ to 10⁻¹ m, ν around 10⁹ to 10¹¹ Hz ✓
Their wavelengths span some **fifteen orders of magnitude**, yet all three cross a
vacuum at exactly the same speed.
**Why the speed is the same.** It is fixed by the **electric and magnetic properties of
free space**, μ₀ and ε₀, not by the source or the wave itself ✓ Maxwell's calculation of
1/√(μ₀ε₀) matching the measured speed of light was the proof that light **is** an
electromagnetic wave.
**The evidence from astronomy.** A gamma-ray burst releases radiation across the whole
spectrum at once, and after billions of years of travel the different wavelengths still
arrive **together** ✓ This limits any difference in speed to better than one part in
10¹⁵.
**What happens in a medium.** There the speeds **do** differ, because the refractive
index depends on frequency ✓ That is **dispersion**, and it is why a prism spreads white
light into a spectrum. The question specifies **vacuum**, where no such effect exists.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Same frequency but different velocities**" ✗ reverses
both facts. "**Same velocity and same frequency**" ✗ would make them the same radiation.
"**Same wavelengths but different velocities**" ✗ is wrong on both counts ✓
∴ same velocity but different wavelengths.

The hydrogen energy levels are **negative** and grow **towards zero** as n rises - so the
energy increases with n.
**Step 1 — write the energy.**
E_n = **−13·6/n² eV** ✓
**Step 2 — tabulate.**
n = 1: **−13·60 eV**
n = 2: **−3·40 eV**
n = 3: **−1·51 eV**
n = ∞: **0** ✓
**Step 3 — read the trend.** Each value is **larger** - less negative - than the one
before, so **the electron's energy increases as n increases** ✓
**Why the energies are negative.** The zero is taken at **infinite separation**, where
the electron is free and at rest ✓ A **bound** electron has less energy than that, so its
energy is negative. The magnitude 13·6 eV is the **ionisation energy** - the work needed
to free a ground-state electron.
**Why a less negative energy means a weaker binding.** Increasing n moves the electron to
a larger, more loosely bound orbit ✓ At n = ∞ it is barely held at all, and beyond that
it is free.
**Testing the other statements.**
"**energy is zero for n = 1**" ✗ - it is −13·6 eV, the most negative value of all.
"**energy varies as n²**" ✗ - it varies as **1/n²**; it is the **radius** that goes as
n² ✓
"**hydrogen emits infrared for ∞ → 1**" ✗ - that transition releases the full **13·6 eV**,
giving λ = 1240/13·6 = **91 nm**, in the far **ultraviolet** ✓ It is the series limit of
the Lyman series, the most energetic line hydrogen can emit.
**Which transitions do give infrared.** Those ending on **n ≥ 3** ✓ The Paschen series
(to n = 3) runs from 820 to 1875 nm, all infrared, because the upper levels are so
closely spaced.
**The pattern of the spacing.** E₂ − E₁ = 10·2 eV, E₃ − E₂ = 1·89 eV, E₄ − E₃ =
0·66 eV ✓ The levels crowd together rapidly, which is why the spectral series converge
to a limit.
∴ electron energy increases as n increases.

**Visible light** is the narrow band the human eye responds to, from about **400 nm to
700 nm**.
**Step 1 — place the band.** Wavelengths from roughly 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red)
are what the retina detects ✓ Outside that range radiation is invisible, however intense.
**Step 2 — see the colours within it.**
violet **400-450 nm**
blue 450-495
green 495-570
yellow 570-590
orange 590-620
red **620-700 nm** ✓
**Step 3 — note the neighbours.**
just **below** 400 nm: **ultraviolet** - invisible, and energetic enough to damage skin
just **above** 700 nm: **infrared** - invisible, felt as heat ✓
**How narrow the visible band is.** The electromagnetic spectrum runs from gamma rays at
10⁻¹² m to radio waves at kilometres - some **eighteen orders of magnitude** ✓ Visible
light occupies less than one **octave** of that, a frequency ratio of under 2 : 1. It is
an extraordinarily small window.
**Why the eye evolved for this band.** It is precisely where the Sun's output peaks at
the Earth's surface, and where the atmosphere and water are most transparent ✓ Evolution
selected the band that carries the most information.
**The corresponding energies.**
700 nm: 1240/700 = **1·77 eV**
400 nm: 1240/400 = **3·10 eV** ✓
a factor of under two across the whole visible range.
**Reading the distractors.** **1 mm to 700 nm** ✗ is the **infrared** region. **400 nm
to 1 nm** ✗ is the **ultraviolet** - the boundary at 400 nm is right, but it extends the
wrong way. **1 nm to 10⁻³ nm** ✗ is the **X-ray** band ✓ Each distractor is a genuine
part of the spectrum, which is what makes the question worth asking: the 400 nm boundary
appears in two of them, and only one has 700 nm at the other end.
∴ 400 nm to 700 nm.

Test the capacitor bridge for **balance** first; if it balances, the middle capacitor
carries no charge and can be removed.
**Step 1 — check the balance condition.** For a capacitor bridge the condition is
C₁/C₂ = C₃/C₄ ✓
Here the two upper arms are 3 and 6, the two lower 4 and 8:
3/6 = **0·5** and 4/8 = **0·5** ✓ equal, so the bridge is **balanced**.
**Step 2 — remove the bridging capacitor.** With the two midpoints at the same
potential, the 2 µF across them has **no potential difference** and therefore **no
charge** ✓ It can be deleted without changing anything.
**Step 3 — reduce the two series arms.**
upper: (3 x 6)/(3 + 6) = 18/9 = **2 µF**
lower: (4 x 8)/(4 + 8) = 32/12 = **8/3 µF** ✓
**Step 4 — combine them in parallel.** Both arms connect A to B:
C_AB = 2 + 8/3
= 6/3 + 8/3
= **14/3 µF** ✓
**Why the balance condition takes this form.** The midpoint potentials are set by the
**ratio** in which each arm divides the applied voltage ✓ For capacitors in series the
voltage divides **inversely** as the capacitances, so equal ratios in the two arms put
the midpoints at the same potential - exactly as equal resistance ratios do in a
Wheatstone bridge.
**Why series capacitors combine like parallel resistors.** 1/C = Σ1/C ✓ Here 3 and 6 in
series give 2, which is **less** than either - the opposite of what resistors do, and
the usual stumbling block.
**A check on the magnitude.** 14/3 = **4·67 µF**, which lies between the 2 µF of the
weaker arm and the sum of the two arms ✓ plausible for a parallel combination.
**Reading the distractors.** **21 µF** ✗ and **23 µF** ✗ are far too large - no
combination of these capacitors can exceed 3 + 6 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 23 µF, and that would
need them all in parallel. **3/14 µF** ✗ is the **reciprocal** of the answer, from
inverting at the wrong stage ✓
∴ 14/3 μF.

A metal sphere in an external field becomes **polarised**, and the field lines must meet
its surface **at right angles** while vanishing inside.
**Step 1 — recall the two rules for a conductor in equilibrium.**
the field **inside** is **zero** ✓
the field just outside is **perpendicular** to the surface ✓
Both follow from the fact that any tangential field would drive charge along the
surface until it was cancelled.
**Step 2 — see what induction does.** The uniform downward field pushes the sphere's
free electrons **upward**, leaving
**negative** charge on the **upper** face
**positive** charge on the **lower** face ✓
The sphere stays neutral overall, but it is now polarised.
**Step 3 — see what that does to the lines.** Field lines approaching the sphere
**terminate** on the induced negative charge on top, and new lines **begin** on the
induced positive charge beneath ✓ No line passes through the metal, and all of them
strike the surface radially.
**Step 4 — see what happens away from the sphere.** The induced charges distort the
field near the sphere, with the lines bending in towards it, while far away the field
is undisturbed and uniform ✓
**Step 5 — match to the figures.** The correct picture shows lines **curving into** the
sphere from above and **out of** it below, meeting the surface perpendicularly, with
**no lines crossing the interior** ✓ That is the third figure.
**Why the lines bend towards the sphere.** A conductor is an equipotential, so the
surrounding equipotential surfaces must wrap around it ✓ Field lines, being
perpendicular to equipotentials, are drawn in - the sphere behaves rather like a short
circuit for the field.
**Why the inside must be empty of lines.** Any field inside would exert a force on the
free electrons and move them ✓ In **electrostatic equilibrium**, by definition, nothing
is moving, so E = 0 throughout the metal. This is the principle of the **Faraday cage**.
**Reading the distractors.** Figures showing lines passing **straight through** the
sphere ✗ violate E = 0 inside. Figures showing lines meeting the surface at an **angle**
✗ violate the perpendicularity condition ✓ Those two tests identify the right picture at
a glance.
∴ the third figure.
